parts.problem_md: Explain **one** way you managed a risk associated with your primary data collection.
parts.solution_md:
Award **1 mark **for a reason further mark for extension through explanation, up to a maximum of **2 marks**:

It allowed find out about the spatial variation in the area of study **(1)** so that we knew that we would get good spatial coverage to minimise bias **(1)**.

Stratified sampling was used as we had census data about the towns population **(1)** so we could design a fair sampling frame for the questionnaire about energy that we were using **(1)**.

Accept any other appropriate response, e.g. asking “different people” is allowable.

parts.problem_md:
Study Figure 9 which was produced by a group of students as part of their investigation of the location of **either** factories or services.

![q9a-june-2018-edexcel-igcse-geography](assets/001-q9a-june-2018-edexcel-igcse-geography.png)

Suggest **one** possible aim of this investigation.

A group of students has undertaken an enquiry that investigated how energy use is changing in Thornfield, a small market town in northern England.

They wanted to find out whether renewable energy adoption was increasing across different parts of the town.

State **one** type of sampling that the students could have used to select their data collection sites.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - Random sampling
> - Systematic sampling
> - Stratified sampling
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> No mark will be awarded for vague answers such as 'fair sampling' or 'good sampling' without a recognised geographical sampling method being named.

parts.problem_md:
The students visited five sites in the small market town of Thornfield and recorded the number of solar panels visible on buildings.

Explain **one **risk that the students may have faced during their fieldwork in Thornfield, and describe how they could have managed it.
parts.solution_md:
One risk was traffic when recording data near roadsides and on busy streets in the town centre. **[1]** The students could have managed this by carrying out a risk assessment before the visit, identifying the most dangerous locations in advance. **[1]** They could also have worked in pairs and stood on the pavement away from the road at all times during data collection. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**explain**' means the answer must go beyond simply naming a risk. The answer must show how the risk was or could have been managed.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for identifying a plausible risk linked to the fieldwork context
> - **One mark** for explaining one way of managing that risk
> - **One further mark** for developing the management strategy
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> **Risks**
> 
> - Uneven or slippery surfaces at the rural fringe or industrial site
> - Adverse weather conditions during outdoor data collection
> - Working near an industrial area with potential hazards
> - Personal safety when working in pairs in unfamiliar locations
> 
> **Management strategies**
> 
> - Wearing high-visibility clothing near roads or industrial areas
> - Informing a responsible adult of the route and timing
> - Checking the weather forecast and dressing appropriately
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Naming a risk without explaining how it was managed
> - Giving a very generic risk such as 'getting lost' without linking it to the Thornfield fieldwork context
> - Describing the risk in detail but neglecting the management strategy entirely

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Structure **your answer in two clear parts:
> 
> - the risk
> - the management
> 
> **The** third mark is always for development of the management strategy, so push your answer one step further than the obvious.
> 
> **Instead **of just saying 'do a risk assessment', say what the risk assessment would identify or what action it would lead to.

parts.problem_md:
The students visited five sites and recorded the number of solar panels visible on buildings. They also completed an environmental quality survey (EQS) at each site, scoring each location out of 10, where 10 represents the highest environmental quality.

**Figure 1: **Solar panel count and environmental quality scores across five sites in Thornfield

| Site | Location type | Number of solar panels recorded | Environmental quality score (out of 10) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Town centre | 3 | 4 |
| 2 | Inner suburb | 8 | 6 |
| 3 | Outer suburb | 19 | 8 |
| 4 | Rural fringe | 24 | 9 |
| 5 | Industrial area | 1 | 3 |

Using **Figure 1,** explain **one **way the students could have used secondary data to support their enquiry into changing energy use in Thornfield.
parts.solution_md:
The students could have used local council planning records **[1]** to find out how many planning applications for solar panel installation had been approved in Thornfield over the past ten years, allowing them to compare the trend in applications with the pattern of solar panels they recorded in Figure 1. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**explain**' means a named secondary source alone is not sufficient. The answer must show how that source would support or extend the fieldwork findings.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for identifying a specific and plausible secondary data source
> - **One mark** for explaining how it would support the enquiry into changing energy use
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Government energy statistics on renewable energy adoption by region
> - Satellite images or historic Google Maps images to track changes in solar panel numbers over time
> - Local newspaper articles reporting on energy schemes in Thornfield
> - Energy company data on households connected to renewable energy tariffs
> 
> No credit will be given for vague sources, such as 'the internet' or 'a website', without further specification.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Naming a secondary source without explaining how it links to the enquiry focus
> - Describing primary data collection methods instead of secondary data
> - Using Figure 1 data as the secondary source (Figure 1 is primary fieldwork data)

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Secondary **data means data collected by someone else, not by you.
> 
> **Always** name the source precisely, then use the word 'because' or 'to compare' to link it to the enquiry.
> 
> **That **second sentence is where your second mark lives.

parts.problem_md:
What conclusions can be reached from an analysis of Figures 9b and 9c?

![q9b-june-2017-edexcel-igcse-geography](assets/005-q9b-june-2017-edexcel-igcse-geography.png)

![q9c-june-2017-edexcel-igcse-geography](assets/006-q9c-june-2017-edexcel-igcse-geography.png)
parts.solution_md:
Figure 9c should show all Figure 9b’s data. Conclusions should relate to this data and data-supported conclusions must receive good credit.

Remember data relates to “against” that source. Credit equally responses that invert data into “for” source e.g. 74% of 16-24 favour nuclear, 98% favour solar ….

Key conclusions can be drawn based on :

1. source overall e.g.

- nuclear is generally least popular source
- solar is generally most popular
- fracking generally less popular than onshore wind

1. age-group e.g.

- renewables i.e. onshore wind and solar far more popular among younger people (16-34) that nuclear and fracking
- fracking more unpopular with older generations e. 35 +
- apart from 45-54s, nuclear similarly unpopular across age-range

older age-groups less keen on renewables than younger. Extent of opposition expected i.e. adjectives (e.g.lot/little/some/most) or data in best answers.

parts.problem_md:
Study Figures 4a and 4b. They show two different data presentation techniques from a student’s fieldwork into energy use.

"The aim of the student’s investigation was to identify attitudes towards the plans for a new nuclear power station in north-west India." The student carried out two different types of surveys into people’s opinions and attitudes towards the proposed energy development.

Evaluate the student’s data presentation techniques.

![fig-4a-4ge1-02r-june-2019-edexcel-igcse-geography](assets/003-fig-4a-4ge1-02r-june-2019-edexcel-igcse-geograph.png)

![fig-4b-4ge1-02r-june-2019-edexcel-igcse-geography](assets/004-fig-4b-4ge1-02r-june-2019-edexcel-igcse-geograph.png)
parts.solution_md:
**Marking instructions**   Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below.

**Indicative content guidance**   The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited.  Relevant points may include:

**AO3 **

- Both Figures 4a and 4b do show some outcomes from the fieldwork surveys, therefore it is possible to make some sense of what the student found.
- Figure 4a seems incomplete as the nature of the questions asked is not present on the key so it’s difficult to draw conclusions.
- Figure 4b only shows one picture , so this might be biased as some could have been missed, therefore this technique is limited in its appropriateness.
- Recognition of issue in presentation (both Figure 4a and b) may be flawed in terms of approach and usage.
- An evaluation of how far the presentation techniques can be trusted may be provided.

**AO4**

- In Figure 4a there is no totals column for the Peoples Responses
- In Figure 4a the is no strongly agree category
- In Figure 4a the colours may be the wrong choice of plot technique
- In Figure 4b only 2 opinions are shown (there may have been more). They may have been edited.
- In Figure 4b there is no idea as to how the responses were selected
- In Figure 4b show anything about the area / context of where the interview took place and when.

parts.problem_md:
Study Figure 9 which was produced by a group of students as part of their investigation of the location of **either** factories or services.

![q9a-june-2018-edexcel-igcse-geography](assets/001-q9a-june-2018-edexcel-igcse-geography.png)

Describe the use of equipment and the field techniques that might have been used when collecting information in this type of investigation.

Equipment

Field techniques
parts.solution_md:
Relevant equipment and techniques obviously depend to some extent on the precise aims of the investigation and so the data that needs to be collected.

There are many possibilities so some examiner discretion will be called for. However, for factory or service industry locations to be investigated the following are generally most likely to be creditable :

Equipment **(4 marks)** – clipboard** (1)**; base map ** (1)**; camera ** (1)**; recording sheets ** (1)**; questionnaire ** (1)**...

Max 1 for stationary

Field techniques **(4 marks) **– sketching ** (1)**; interviewing ** (1)**; recording ** (1) **individual and/or group work ** (1)** …

Accept sampling techniques in this section.

In each case, max of 3 marks where the use of equipment/technique was not described/developed but merely identified. 4 marks are available for each aspect of the question and max marks in each case require some description of use e.g. max marks can be awarded where 2 pieces of equipment and 2 field techniques are identified and then described as to how they can be used in the field to collect factory/services location data/information.
